title: ACE-inhibitor (bradykinin) angioedema
summary: Deep swelling of the lips, tongue or face without wheals or itch in a patient on an ACE inhibitor, which can start years into treatment and does not respond to antihistamines.

glance.think: Recurrent lip, tongue or face swelling without hives in someone on ramipril, lisinopril or another ACE inhibitor.
glance.engine: ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown; bradykinin leaks fluid into deep tissue, so histamine-based treatments work poorly.
glance.backbone: Airway first (999 if needed); stop the ACE inhibitor permanently and record it; choose a non-ACE alternative with care.
glance.never_miss: Airway compromise; hereditary angioedema; ARB or sacubitril/valsartan cross-reactivity; DPP-4 inhibitors raising the risk.

what: Episodic, non-pitting swelling of the deep dermis/submucosa (lips, tongue, face, larynx, gut) **without wheals or itch**, caused by ACE inhibitors. It affects ~0.1–0.7% of users and accounts for up to a third of angioedema presentations to emergency departments. It can start **at any time — from the first dose to years later** (often within the first months).

list: ACE (kininase II) normally breaks down **bradykinin**. ACE inhibition → bradykinin (and substance P) accumulate → **B2 receptors** → vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability. It is **not histamine- or IgE-mediated**, which is why antihistamines, steroids and often adrenaline don't work.

**Risk factors:** **black ethnicity** (≈3–5×), female sex, age >65, smoking, previous idiopathic angioedema, seasonal allergies, and **co-prescription of DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins)**, mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus), **sacubitril/valsartan** (neprilysin inhibition — contraindicated within 36 h of an ACE-i) or alteplase.
**Triggers:** minor trauma/surgery, dental work and intubation can precipitate attacks. That fits this case (swelling a week after skin-tag removal), though the procedure is a trigger, not the cause.

features: Face, periorbital tissue, lips, **tongue**, floor of mouth and larynx; recurrent intestinal angioedema (abdominal pain). Swelling develops over hours and lasts **24–72 h**. Attacks may recur for weeks after stopping the ACE-i (the effect wanes over ~1–3 months), so the episodes that follow are not "treatment failure".

list: Clinical: angioedema with **no urticaria**, on an ACE-i, not responding to antihistamine/steroid.

**Investigations:** Usually none are needed to diagnose it; **C4** (+ C1-inhibitor level and function) if there is no ACE-i, a family history, onset before 40, or recurrence after stopping — to exclude **hereditary/acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency** (C4 low in both). In acquired deficiency, look for lymphoproliferative disease and C1q; **Mast-cell tryptase** if anaphylaxis is possible; FBC/TFT if chronic urticaria is in the differential

head: Histamine (allergic/mast-cell) angioedema
Bradykinin angioedema (ACE-i, HAE)
rows: **C4 low in HAE/AAE**; normal in ACE-i

differentials: Also: contact dermatitis of the eyelids/face, cellulitis/erysipelas, SVC obstruction, hypothyroid myxoedema, Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome / orofacial granulomatosis, dermatomyositis (periorbital oedema — the [skin signs of systemic disease](condition:dermatomyositis) notes).

ol: **Airway first.** Tongue, floor-of-mouth or laryngeal swelling, voice change, stridor or dysphagia → **999 / ED**. Adrenaline is given if anaphylaxis cannot be excluded. In hospital, airway management is the priority; off-label icatibant, C1-INH concentrate or fresh frozen plasma are sometimes used (evidence is mixed — RCTs of icatibant in ACE-i angioedema were negative).
**Stop ramipril permanently** and record "**ACE inhibitor — angioedema (class reaction): avoid all ACE inhibitors**". Do not rechallenge. Yellow Card.

**Alternative for hypertension/T2DM renoprotection (NICE NG136/NG28):** An **ARB** can be considered **with caution**. Recurrence on ARBs is uncommon (~2–10% in studies), so discuss with the patient, consider specialist advice, and safety-net; Or use a **calcium-channel blocker** (amlodipine), with an SGLT2 inhibitor for renal protection where indicated
**Avoid** sacubitril/valsartan, and think twice before adding a **gliptin** (DPP-4 inhibitors also reduce bradykinin/substance-P breakdown).
**Explain** that swelling may recur for several weeks after stopping. Stop cetirizine/prednisolone if they gave no benefit (avoid steroid harm in new diabetes — hyperglycaemia).
**Metformin and simvastatin** are not implicated and can continue.

management: Airway involvement (999); recurrent angioedema without an ACE-i, or with a family history (immunology — C4/C1-INH); abdominal attacks; angioedema persisting >3 months after stopping.
Recognise, stop and switch the ACE-i (within competence for hypertension/diabetes), document the class allergy, Yellow Card, safety-net. Immunology referral for suspected HAE/AAE.
red_flags: Tongue or throat swelling, voice change, stridor or difficulty swallowing: **999** now.
Stop the ACE inhibitor **permanently** even if the swelling has settled, and document it as an adverse reaction.
pearls: "Angioedema **without wheals** on an ACE-i = bradykinin. Antihistamines won't fix it — **stopping the ACE-i** will (eventually)."
Check every ACE-i patient on the medication review for previous facial or tongue swelling — patients often don't link it to a long-standing tablet.
The risk persists for years on treatment, so this is not just a "first-month" issue.
